hook.line: Tomás is brave about the café but not about his Spanish. When he talks about what scares him, Spanish has a tidy way to say it.
hook.en: I'm afraid of getting it wrong.

examples.en: I'm afraid of getting it wrong.

examples.es: A Tomás le da miedo hablar con los clientes.
Rosa tenía miedo a perder el café.
examples.en: Rosa was afraid of losing the café.

examples.es: Hernando tiene miedo de quedarse solo.
examples.en: Hernando is afraid of being left alone.

rule:
Two ways to say what you're afraid of:

*Tengo miedo a* + what scares you: *Tengo miedo a las alturas.*
*Me da miedo* + what scares you: *Le da miedo manejar.* (*A Tomás le da miedo hablar.*)

After *miedo*, a verb stays as an infinitive: *miedo a perder*. English says *of losing*; Spanish says *a perder*.

You'll hear *miedo de* too, with the same meaning: *miedo de quedarse solo*.

This is for your own fear. Someone else's action takes a longer pattern, coming later.
smallPrint: Teachers call this a noun complement: *miedo* takes *a* or *de*, then an infinitive when the person afraid is also the one doing it.

options: I'm afraid of getting it wrong.
I'm afraid you'll get it wrong.

readAndPick.es: Rosa tenía miedo a perder el café.
options: Rosa is afraid of losing the café.
Rosa was afraid of losing the café.

readAndPick.es: Hernando tiene miedo de quedarse solo.
options: Hernando is afraid of being left alone.
Hernando is afraid of the dark.

readAndPick.es: A Tomás le da miedo hablar con los clientes.
options: Tomás is afraid to talk to the customers.
The customers are afraid of Tomás.

readAndPick.es: Mi papá tiene miedo de volar.
options: My dad is afraid of flying.
My dad is afraid of flights.

readAndPick.es: Nos da miedo perder la cuadra.
options: The block is afraid of losing us.
I'm afraid of nothing at all.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *Tengo miedo ___ equivocarme.* (*a* or *por*) I'm afraid of getting it wrong.
yourTurn.why: *Miedo* links to what scares you with *a* (or *de*), then an infinitive.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *___ da miedo manejar.* (*Le* or *Les*) Driving scares her.
yourTurn.why: She is one person, so *le*; the fear is what gets done to her.
A thing that scares you follows *miedo a*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: Rosa was afraid of losing the café.
yourTurn.answer: Rosa tenía miedo a perder el café.
accept: Rosa tenía miedo de perder el café.
yourTurn.why: A past fear uses *tenía*, then *a* and the infinitive.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: Losing the block scares us.
yourTurn.answer: Nos da miedo perder la cuadra.
yourTurn.why: *Nos* means us, and *perder* stays as an infinitive.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: My dad is afraid of flying.
yourTurn.answer: Mi papá tiene miedo de volar.
accept: Mi papá tiene miedo a volar.
Mi papá le tiene miedo a volar.
yourTurn.why: *Tiene* matches one person, then *de* or *a* and the infinitive.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: *Tengo miedo a hablar en público.*
yourTurn.answer: No tengo miedo a hablar en público.
accept: No tengo miedo de hablar en público.
yourTurn.why: Put *no* in front of *tengo*; nothing else changes.

pitfalls.why: Almost. In Spanish you *have* fear, with *tengo*, instead of being afraid.
After *a*, a verb stays as an infinitive, not *-ando*.

pitfalls.wrong: Tengo miedo de a perder el café.
pitfalls.right: Tengo miedo a perder el café.

personal: Say two things that scare you, one with *Tengo miedo a…* and one with *Me da miedo…*, each followed by a verb in the infinitive.
